issues.item: Memory: Verbal Access: I can talk about what happened very easily.
issues.explanation: Within the Memory node, 'I can talk about what happened very easily' conflicts with the same node's strong intrusive, poorly controlled re-experiencing items ('triggered without warning' and 'full sensory reliving'). Severe reliving can coexist with disclosure, but 'very easily' pulls in the opposite direction and is the clearest within-node inconsistency.

issues.item: Memory: Triggered Without Warning: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning
issues.explanation: The cognitive formulation leaves Threat disconnected from the active network, yet 'Hypervigilance: I have to be on guard all the time' implies a strong ongoing sense of current threat. That threat-focused appraisal is not supported by the formulation and is not matched by any Threat-node content.

issues.item: Memory: Full Sensory Reliving: When the memory comes back it feels completely real across all my senses at once
issues.explanation: 'Entrapment: Having no options' as a trigger is hard to reconcile with the rest of the profile. The negative appraisals and memory content center on global damage/self-reliance and sensory reliving, not on themes of being trapped or unable to escape, so this trigger appears insufficiently grounded in the reported formulation.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Hypervigilance: I have to be on guard all the time
issues.explanation: 'Avoid Physical Stress' is weakly supported by the rest of the profile. The triggers and appraisals do not indicate body-strain or exertion as a salient trauma-linked theme, making this strategy look disconnected from the reported trigger-memory-appraisal pattern.

The trigger profile is centered on entrapment, touch, and a specific taste, which implies reactivity to concrete sensory or situational reminders of the witnessed trauma. 'Entrapment: Having no options' is harder to reconcile with the rest of the profile because the memory and appraisal items do not describe being trapped or immobilized; they emphasize sensory reliving, nonverbal memory, hypervigilance, and global damage/self-doubt rather than a trapped-state theme. For a witnessed-trauma case, this item stands out as poorly integrated with the rest of the formulation.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Physical Stress: Situations that put my body under stress
issues.explanation: 'Avoid Physical Stress' is not well supported by the rest of the five-component profile. The selected triggers and memory items point to sensory cue-driven reliving, and the appraisals concern vigilance, self-reliance, and life damage. Avoiding bodily stress suggests fear of physiological arousal or somatic activation, but there are no corresponding threat or appraisal items about bodily danger, losing control when activated, or physical collapse. It therefore looks like a maladaptive strategy targeting a symptom pattern not otherwise represented in the profile.

issues.item: Avoid Reminders: Being reminded of the event by others
issues.explanation: 'Avoid Reminders' appears mis-keyed: the strategy should be an avoidant behavior (e.g., avoiding being reminded), but the selected text describes a trigger/reminder rather than something the patient does. This makes the maladaptive-strategy item internally incoherent.

issues.item: Hypervigilance: I have to be on guard all the time
issues.explanation: The profile includes a prominent current-threat appraisal ('I have to be on guard all the time') despite Threat being structurally inactive: there are no active edges to or from Threat, and the rest of the profile is dominated by memory-based reexperiencing, negative self-appraisals, and coping strategies rather than an active external-danger formulation. This item fits Threat more than Negative Appraisals and is inconsistent with the specified formulation.

vignette:
Marcus was twenty-eight when the accident happened on a Tuesday afternoon in late September. He had been framing the second story of a residential renovation in Arlington, Virginia—a job he'd bid competitively and was determined to finish ahead of schedule. His crew that day consisted of himself, a newer guy named Derek who was still learning the trade, and Tom, a seasoned carpenter in his sixties who'd worked alongside Marcus for nearly a decade. They were installing headers above a load-bearing wall when Tom stepped backward to check the level of a beam. His boot caught the edge of an open floor joist. In the three seconds it took for him to fall, Marcus watched his body rotate in the air. Tom landed on his left side on the concrete subfloor below—a drop of twelve feet. The sound was not what Marcus expected. It was wet and wrong. When Marcus reached him, Tom's left arm was bent at an angle that made no anatomical sense, and there was blood pooling beneath his head, a metallic taste suddenly present in Marcus's mouth as if he'd bitten his own tongue, though he hadn't.

The emergency response, the hospital waiting room, Tom's wife arriving in shock—all of it became a kind of blur that Marcus could not quite convert into a coherent story. When he tried to explain it to his wife, Keisha, in the days that followed, the words would not come. He could see it all with perfect clarity: the angle of Tom's arm, the blood, the taste. But when he opened his mouth, nothing emerged that felt true. It was as if the event existed only in his body, in the sensations that kept replaying without his permission. Tom survived, but with a traumatic brain injury and a shattered humerus. He would not return to carpentry. Marcus carried the weight of that knowledge through the winter. By January, two months after the fall, he had developed a pattern he did not fully recognize until Keisha pointed it out: whenever he felt the memory rising—that taste, that image—he would reach for food. Late at night, he would stand in the kitchen and eat an entire box of cereal, or a half-gallon of ice cream, not tasting it, not wanting it, but needing the sensation of fullness, the physical act of swallowing, something to anchor him to the present moment. He gained twenty-three pounds. His clothes no longer fit. He stopped looking at himself in the mirror.

The job sites became increasingly difficult. In March, while installing trim in a new construction, a subcontractor cut his hand on sheet metal. The blood—bright red, vivid—triggered the memory so completely that Marcus lost twenty minutes. He found himself sitting in his truck with no memory of how he'd gotten there, his hands shaking, his body drenched in sweat. He'd been somewhere else entirely. He came to believe that his mind was no longer trustworthy, that it could leave him at any moment without warning. The taste would come unbidden: metallic, copper-tinged, appearing in his mouth when he was eating lunch or kissing Keisha goodnight. When it came, he would dissociate deliberately, trying to leave his body, to blank out the sensation. Sometimes he would succeed; other times he would be stuck between two realities—present but not present, aware of Keisha speaking to him but unable to respond, as if he were behind thick glass. He also found himself unable to concentrate on the technical details of his work; his mind would scatter when he tried to calculate measurements or follow blueprints, as though the accident had fractured his ability to hold information in his head.

By summer, Marcus had stopped accepting new contracts. He told clients he was overscheduled. The truth was that he could not trust himself on a job site. He'd watched another carpenter take a fall from a ladder in early June—nothing serious, just a stumble—but the sight of the man's bloodied knee had sent Marcus into a dissociative state that lasted hours. His reputation in the local construction community, built over a decade, began to quietly erode. Keisha, who worked in medical administration, found herself increasingly the sole income earner. They had been saving for a down payment on a house. That plan was now indefinite. What finally brought Marcus to a therapist's office in late August, now thirty years old, was not a crisis but an accumulation: the weight gain, the distance that had grown between him and Keisha, the knowledge that he could not return to the work that had defined him. He sat in the intake session, unable to fully articulate why he was there, knowing only that his life had fundamentally broken and that he no longer recognized himself in it. He was terrified that this was permanent—that the man he'd been before Tom's fall was gone forever, and that the person he'd become was someone he could no longer rely on to function.
